\chapter{The Weather}
\label{ch:spanish-weather}
\hlchaptermodality{93}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can talk about the weather in Spanish and know why llueve refuses to join hace.}

Ask about el tiempo, answer hace calor, hace frío, hace sol, then switch to llueve — a verb of its own, whose ll- is the same sound change that gave llamar.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el tiempo]{el tiempo — one word doing two jobs}

\label{lesson:ES-C30-el-tiempo}



\begin{quote}
Ask a Spanish speaker \emph{¿qué tiempo hace?} and you are literally asking \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{what time does it make?}\textquotedblright{} — because \emph{tiempo} does not split \textquotedblleft{}time\textquotedblright{} from \textquotedblleft{}weather\textquotedblright{} the way English does.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el tiempo} = both \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{time}\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{weather}\textquotedblright{} — from Latin \textbf{tempus}, which already carried this same double sense. Nothing was merged in Spanish; the two meanings simply arrived together and stayed.

English inherited the word too, through borrowing, but kept \textbf{only the time half}: \textbf{temporal}, \textbf{contemporary}, \textbf{tempo}, \textbf{temporary}. So the double meaning is not a Spanish oddity — it is the older state of affairs, and English is the one that narrowed.

How does a Spanish speaker know which is meant? \textbf{Context alone}, and it is never ambiguous in practice: \emph{no tengo tiempo} is \textquotedblleft{}I have no time,\textquotedblright{} \emph{¿qué tiempo hace?} is \textquotedblleft{}what's the weather like?\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}el tiempo\textquotedblright{} — time, or weather, depending on context
  \item \textquotedblleft{}¿qué tiempo hace?\textquotedblright{} — what's the weather like?
  \item \textquotedblleft{}tiempo\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}tempo, temporal\textquotedblright{} — the \emph{tempus} family
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two things does \textbf{el tiempo} mean? (\textbf{Time} and \textbf{weather}.) Which Latin word gives it, and did it already mean both? (\textbf{Tempus} — yes, both.) Which language narrowed the meaning, Spanish or English? (\textbf{English} — it kept only \textquotedblleft{}time.\textquotedblright{}) Next: how to actually answer \emph{¿qué tiempo hace?}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hace calor, hace frío, hace sol]{hace calor, hace frío, hace sol — the weather Spanish \emph{makes}}

\label{lesson:ES-C30-hace-calor}



\begin{quote}
You can ask \emph{¿qué tiempo hace?} Now answer it. Three of Spanish's commonest weather answers all take the same verb you already know — \emph{hacer}, \textquotedblleft{}to make.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{calor} $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{calor}, \textquotedblleft{}heat, warmth\textquotedblright{} $\to$ English \textbf{calorie}, \textbf{caloric}, \textbf{cauldron}.
  \item \textbf{frío} $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{frigidus}, \textquotedblleft{}cold\textquotedblright{} (the middle syllable syncopated away) $\to$ English \textbf{frigid}, \textbf{refrigerate}.
  \item \textbf{sol} $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{sol}, \textquotedblleft{}sun,\textquotedblright{} unchanged $\to$ English \textbf{solar}, \textbf{solstice}, \textbf{parasol}.
\end{itemize}

Here is the part worth noticing: all three are \textbf{nouns}, not adjectives. \emph{Calor} is \textquotedblleft{}heat,\textquotedblright{} not \textquotedblleft{}hot.\textquotedblright{} That is exactly why Spanish reaches for \textbf{hacer}: you cannot \emph{be} a noun, but the world can \textbf{make} one.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{hace calor} — \textquotedblleft{}it's hot,\textquotedblright{} literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{it makes heat}\textquotedblright{} \textbf{hace frío} — \textquotedblleft{}it's cold,\textquotedblright{} literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{it makes cold}\textquotedblright{} \textbf{hace sol} — \textquotedblleft{}it's sunny,\textquotedblright{} literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{it makes sun}\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

French does the same thing with the same logic (\emph{il fait chaud}); English is the outlier, forcing weather into \textquotedblleft{}it \textbf{is} hot\textquotedblright{} with an adjective.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hace calor. hace frío. hace sol.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the literal reading — \textquotedblleft{}it makes heat, it makes cold, it makes sun\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}calor\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}calorie\textquotedblright{}; \textquotedblleft{}frío\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}refrigerate\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}it's hot,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}it's cold,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}it's sunny.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Hace calor, hace frío, hace sol}.) Why does Spanish use \emph{hacer} rather than a \textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{} verb? (Because \emph{calor}, \emph{frío} and \emph{sol} are \textbf{nouns} — the weather \textbf{makes} heat, it does not \emph{be} hot.) Give an English cousin of \emph{frío}. (\textbf{Frigid}, \textbf{refrigerate}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[llueve]{llueve — the one weather word that will not join \emph{hacer}}

\label{lesson:ES-C30-llueve}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Hace calor, hace frío, hace sol} — three answers, one pattern. Now try rain, and the pattern breaks. Rain does not get made in Spanish; rain has a verb of its own.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: rain brings its own verb}]
\textbf{llueve} = \textquotedblleft{}it's raining.\textquotedblright{} Not \emph{hace lluvia}, not \textquotedblleft{}it makes rain\textquotedblright{} — just \textbf{llueve}, a single word that is a complete sentence.

It comes from \textbf{llover}, \textquotedblleft{}to rain,\textquotedblright{} and \emph{llover} is \textbf{impersonal}: it has no subject at all, not even a \textquotedblleft{}it\textquotedblright{} you could point to. Compare the two shapes side by side:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{pattern} & \textbf{example} & \textbf{what carries the weather} \\
\midrule
\textbf{hacer} + noun & \emph{hace calor} & the \textbf{noun} (\emph{calor}, heat) \\
dedicated verb & \emph{llueve} & the \textbf{verb itself} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

English does exactly the same split, which makes it easy to feel: you say \textquotedblleft{}it \textbf{is} hot\textquotedblright{} with an adjective, but \textquotedblleft{}it \textbf{rains}\textquotedblright{} with a verb built for the job. Spanish just draws the line in the same place.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{llover} $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{pluere}, \textquotedblleft{}to rain.\textquotedblright{} Recognise that \textbf{pl- $\to$ ll-} shift? It is the \textbf{same regular sound change} that gave you \textbf{llamar} ($\leftarrow$ \emph{clamāre}), \textbf{llave} ($\leftarrow$ \emph{clāvem}, \textquotedblleft{}key\textquotedblright{}) and \textbf{llama} ($\leftarrow$ \emph{flamma}, \textquotedblleft{}flame\textquotedblright{}). Latin's \emph{cl-}, \emph{fl-} and \emph{pl-} clusters all became Spanish \emph{ll-}.

So \emph{llueve} is not an exception you have to memorise twice: it is a predictable descendant of \emph{pluere} (the same root English keeps in \textbf{pluvial} and the \textbf{pluviometer}, a rain gauge), and it is the one weather word with enough of its own life to refuse the \emph{hacer} frame.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}¿qué tiempo hace?\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}hace calor. hace frío. hace sol.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}llueve\textquotedblright{} — one word, a whole sentence, no \emph{hacer}
  \item the family — \textquotedblleft{}llamar, llave, llama, llover\textquotedblright{} — four Latin clusters, one Spanish \emph{ll-}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which weather word does \textbf{not} use \emph{hacer}, and why? (\textbf{Llueve} — rain has its own impersonal verb, \emph{llover}.) What Latin word is \emph{llover} from? (\textbf{Pluere}.) What sound change turned its \emph{pl-} into \emph{ll-}, and what other words show it? (Latin \emph{cl-/fl-/pl-} $\to$ Spanish \emph{ll-} — \emph{llamar}, \emph{llave}, \emph{llama}.) And what does \emph{el tiempo} mean? (\textbf{Time} and \textbf{weather}, from \emph{tempus}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
